The celebration honors deceased loved ones through vibrant altars adorned with marigold flowers (cempasúchil), sugar skulls, pan de muerto (bread of the dead), photographs, and personal items of the departed. Families often visit cemeteries where they clean gravesites, offer food and drink to the spirits of their ancestors, and share stories about them.

While it is most prominently celebrated in Mexico, Día de los Muertos has gained recognition worldwide and is observed in various forms across Central America, South America, and even parts of the United States. Its cultural significance was recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.
